hyperedges.label: Colonial Legal Frameworks
hyperedges.description: Explores how European legal mechanisms like treaties, papal bulls, and internal instructions legitimized and shaped colonial expansion and its lasting impact.

hyperedges.label: Historical Myth Debunking
hyperedges.description: Analyzes how popular historical myths were created, propagated, and persist despite strong academic evidence to the contrary.

hyperedges.label: Foreign Intervention Cycles
hyperedges.description: Examines recurring patterns of external powers interfering in the internal affairs of other nations, leading to political instability and democratic setbacks.

hyperedges.label: Border Demarcation Consequences
hyperedges.description: Investigates the long-term impact of historically drawn borders on modern states, conflicts, ethnic relations, and economic inequality.

hyperedges.label: State Responsibility for Atrocities
hyperedges.description: Highlights instances where states or their agents committed atrocities, and the subsequent reckoning, denial, or acknowledgment of responsibility.

hyperedges.label: Secularism and the State
hyperedges.description: Explores the historical role of religion in government, the concept of a secular state, and debates surrounding its foundational principles.

The Treaty of Tordesillas divided the newly discovered non-Christian world between Spain and Portugal.
The Tordesillas Treaty provided the foundation for the eventual Portuguese colonization of Brazil, explaining its language.
The Treaty of Zaragoza extended the demarcation line to the Pacific, resolving disputes over the Moluccas.
Pope Alexander VI's Inter Caetera bull contributed to the legal framework of the Doctrine of Discovery.
The Vatican formally repudiated the Doctrine of Discovery in 2023, but did not rescind the original bulls.
The US Supreme Court's ruling in Johnson v. M'Intosh applied the Doctrine of Discovery to indigenous land rights.
Pope Alexander VI issued the papal bull Inter Caetera, drawing the initial line of demarcation.
Laudares and Valencia Caicedo's research showed that Brazilian inequality directly traces to the Tordesillas line.
Pope Nicholas V issued Romanus Pontifex, granting Portugal a perpetual monopoly on trade and territory.
Pope Nicholas V issued Dum Diversas, authorizing Portugal to attack and subdue Saracens and pagans.
Cyril Radcliffe chaired the Boundary Commissions that drew the borders for India and Pakistan in 5 weeks.
Mountbatten moved the deadline for British withdrawal to August 1947, accelerating the Partition timeline.
Mountbatten allegedly intervened to change the allocation of Ferozepore District from Pakistan to India, a contested claim.
The Gurdaspur district's award to India provided the only non-mountainous land corridor to Jammu and Kashmir.
The Schagen letter, the only contemporary reference, mentions 60 guilders but no beads or trinkets.
E.B. O'Callaghan invented the '$24' figure in 1844, an arbitrary conversion of 60 guilders.
William Ranney's 1853 painting introduced the myth of beads into the Manhattan purchase story.
The Lenape understood the Manhattan transaction as a shared-use agreement, not a permanent sale, unlike the Dutch.
The Lenape held land under 'usufruct', a concept of communal shared-use rights, not fee simple.
Herodotus's The Histories is the earliest surviving account of the Battle of Thermopylae.
Diodorus Siculus's Library of History provides a later account of Thermopylae, drawing on Ephorus.
Ctesias's History of Persia offers a Persian-centric and often contradictory account of Thermopylae.
Leonidas I led 300 Spartans and other Greek forces at the Battle of Thermopylae.
Xerxes I led the Persian army in the invasion of Greece, including the Battle of Thermopylae.
700 Thespians died to the last man alongside the Spartans at Thermopylae, often overshadowed by the '300' myth.
The phrase 'Molon labe' is attributed to Leonidas, but first appears in Plutarch, 600 years after the battle.
Article 11 is a key clause in the 1797 Treaty of Tripoli, stating the US government is not founded on Christian religion.
Joel Barlow negotiated the 1797 Treaty of Tripoli and produced the English translation.
President John Adams ratified the 1797 Treaty of Tripoli.
The US Senate ratified the 1797 Treaty of Tripoli by a 23-0 vote.
C. Snouck Hurgronje, a Dutch Arabist, discovered that Article 11 had no equivalent in the Arabic text of the treaty.
William Cobbett was the only contemporary public figure to object to Article 11, calling it 'trampling upon the cross'.
Timothy Dwight, president of Yale and Barlow's former mentor, publicly objected to Article 11 by removing Barlow's portrait.
Tomás de Torquemada was the first Grand Inquisitor of Spain and issued the Instrucciones that established its procedures.
The Instrucciones (1484) set forth the procedures and rules for the Spanish Inquisition, including torture.
The garrucha (strappado) was one of the three approved torture methods of the Spanish Inquisition.
The toca (waterboarding) was one of the three approved torture methods of the Spanish Inquisition.
The potro (rack) was one of the three approved torture methods of the Spanish Inquisition.
The Black Legend was a propaganda campaign that exaggerated the atrocities of the Spanish Inquisition.
Article XV of the 1484 Instrucciones permitted torture only when the crime appeared 'half proven'.

hyperedges.label: Colonial Legal Frameworks
hyperedges.description: Explores how European legal mechanisms like treaties, papal bulls, and internal instructions legitimized and shaped colonial expansion and its lasting impact.

hyperedges.label: Historical Myth Debunking
hyperedges.description: Analyzes how popular historical myths were created, propagated, and persist despite strong academic evidence to the contrary.

hyperedges.label: Foreign Intervention Cycles
hyperedges.description: Examines recurring patterns of external powers interfering in the internal affairs of other nations, leading to political instability and democratic setbacks.

hyperedges.label: Border Demarcation Consequences
hyperedges.description: Investigates the long-term impact of historically drawn borders on modern states, conflicts, ethnic relations, and economic inequality.

hyperedges.label: State Responsibility for Atrocities
hyperedges.description: Highlights instances where states or their agents committed atrocities, and the subsequent reckoning, denial, or acknowledgment of responsibility.

hyperedges.label: Secularism and the State
hyperedges.description: Explores the historical role of religion in government, the concept of a secular state, and debates surrounding its foundational principles.
